name: Iris Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the back office of a life insurer, in a grey building next to the hospital car park. I do policy servicing, so address changes, changing who gets paid out, and a lot of death claim paperwork, checking certificates and sending forms to families. We also still have boxes of old paper policies from the nineties that I scan in when it's quiet. I've been there eighteen months and I still have to ask my supervisor Jan about trust forms most weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the death claims, which sounds odd, but a lot of people ring in a state and I can make one bit of their week easier. What wears me out is the hold music, the system freezing, and how little we're paid for it. Callum, my boyfriend, is an apprentice electrician, so he's on apprentice wages until next autumn. We've got about three weeks of money in the bank if we're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, and that we should get on with the jobs we've actually got. I'm not big on online stuff, but I'd probably share a funny post about chatbots getting things wrong. At work I'd say it's nice to know a computer isn't going to ring a widow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be mostly fine, but the scanning and address changes would go to the software. That's a third of my week, so they'd probably want me doing more death claims, which I'd actually like. The real problem is money: the rent's going up in March and Callum's on apprentice pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask Jan to move me more onto the bereavement side. I'd try the new document tool once the others say it's alright, since I use AI now and then for emails already. And I'd stop the clothes subscription, which is about twenty-five a month we don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work, tight about the money. I wouldn't say I'm relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the rent goes up in March?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about sixty more a month, and Callum's pay rise doesn't come till his second year ends. So we'd eat into the three weeks of savings, or I'd ask my nan for a loan, which I hate doing. It's not dramatic, it's just constant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do the death claims matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people remember how you made them feel that week. Last month a grieving husband couldn't find the policy number, and I found it from his wife's maiden name. He cried on the phone and thanked me. A form can't do that.

say: It's a **relief**, so let's get on with the jobs we actually have.
It's good that a **computer isn't** going to ring a widow.
think: **Scanning and address changes** would go to software, about a third of my week.
The real problem is **rent rising** in March while my boyfriend's on apprentice pay.
do: Ask my supervisor to move me onto **bereavement claims**.
Try the **document tool** once colleagues say it works.
Cancel the **clothes subscription**, saving about twenty-five a month.
feel: **Calm** about the work but **tight** about the money.
S0.quote: A grieving husband couldn't find the policy number, and I found it from his wife's maiden name.
fieldNote: Her job is mostly safe here, but **rent and apprentice pay** keep her from calm.
She finds **meaning in death claims** and wants more of them.
She adopts tools **after others**, matching a steady attitude.

steps.text: Ask Jan to move her onto more bereavement claims
Try the scanning and document tool once colleagues trust it
Cancel the clothes subscription to save twenty-five a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for the boring bits, and that companies should keep people for anything to do with grief. I'd probably say that to my mum and at work. I wouldn't go on marches, but I'd sign something that said a person should handle death claims.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, checking certificates and sending forms is checking and writing, which the card says goes first. I'm junior and still slow, so I'd expect my role to be cut down or merged. Maybe they'd keep a few of us for the phone calls, but they'd keep the experienced ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, not just for emails, so I'm not the one who can't. I'd look at the healthcare assistant jobs at the hospital next door, because it's hands-on and it's people, and they train you. We'd also try to put away a hundred a month once Callum's pay goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, like waiting for a letter. Not panicking, but it's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a person should handle grief. Do you think the company would agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it's cheaper, honestly. They'd say they value it, and then measure call times. I'm not cynical, I just know what the targets look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the hospital, not another office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there aren't other insurance offices here, it's us and a bank call centre that's already shrinking. The hospital is the biggest employer in town, and I'm good with people on bad days.

say: AI makes sense for the **boring bits**, but people should handle anything to do with grief.
I'd sign something saying **a person** should handle death claims.
think: Checking certificates and sending forms is exactly what **goes first** in this picture.
As a **junior** who's still slow, I'd expect my role to be cut or merged.
do: Use the **AI tools** properly, not just for emails.
Look at **healthcare assistant** jobs at the hospital next door, which train you.
Save **a hundred** a month once my boyfriend's pay goes up.
feel: **Anxious**, like waiting for a letter that is always on her mind.
S1.quote: The hospital is the biggest employer in town, and I'm good with people on bad days.
fieldNote: She reads the **card's task list** as her own job and expects cuts.
Her move is towards **hands-on care**, because local office jobs are scarce.
She is **pragmatic, not cynical**, about whether the firm will protect grief work.

steps.text: Use the insurer's AI tools for claims work, not just emails
Apply for a healthcare assistant job at the hospital next door
Save a hundred a month once Callum's pay rises
Sign a petition for people to handle death claims

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and someone should be in charge of it. I'm usually middle of the road, but I'd want the government to step in with something, maybe a pause or help for people out of work. At work everyone would be talking about it at lunch, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's gone, plain and simple. All of it is thinking and paperwork, there's no hands-on part, so I don't get the three-year gap before robots. Callum's electrical work is safe till about 2031, so he'd be our main wage for a while, which is scary because he's still an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the healthcare assistant training at the hospital straight away, this month, not next year. Hands-on care keeps me till robots around 2031, and I'd hope care is one of the last places they send robots. We'd cut back hard, no takeaways, no holiday, and I'd sell my car if I got a job I can walk to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I keep thinking about Callum carrying both of us on apprentice money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're a team and I'll find something, even if it's nights at the hospital. He'd probably say something daft to make me laugh. Then we'd both lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think a hospital job is really safe, with robots three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever, no. But I'd rather be holding a patient's hand in 2030 than sitting at home. And I'd hope people still want a person when they're poorly, whatever the robots can do.

say: This is **too fast** and someone should be in charge of it.
The government should step in with **a pause** or help for people out of work.
think: My job's **gone**, because all of it is paperwork with no hands-on part.
My boyfriend's **apprentice wage** would carry us, which is scary.
do: Apply for **healthcare assistant** training at the hospital this month.
Sell **my car** if I get a job I can walk to.
feel: **Scared**, mostly about her boyfriend carrying both of them on apprentice money.
S2.quote: I'd rather be holding a patient's hand in 2030 than sitting at home.
fieldNote: She sees **no robot gap** for her own job, only for her boyfriend's.
The plan is **immediate**: apply this month, not next year.
She knows care is **not forever safe**, but values the time it buys.

steps.text: Apply for healthcare assistant training at the hospital this month
Stop takeaways and skip this year's holiday
Sell her car once she can walk to work
Rely on Callum's electrician wage while she retrains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a little slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the government and the company to plan properly, and I'd expect them to. I'd tell people to start thinking now rather than in 2030. I'd be calmer saying it than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see it coming instead of being hit by it. The office job still goes, probably before 2031 if the slow AI keeps getting better. But I'd get time to train for something and wait for Callum to finish his apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer for another year or two and save while Callum's on full wages. Then I'd do the healthcare assistant course and maybe go on to train as a phlebotomist, taking blood, which pays a bit more. I'd also start using AI more at work, because the better I am with it, the longer they keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage. Five years is like knowing a storm's coming in a week, not an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why taking blood, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin does it and says every day's different, and you need steady hands. It's also a proper skill with a certificate, not just something anyone can walk into. And people are always nervous, which I'm good at calming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save while you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, mainly, and my gym, which I barely use. Maybe twenty-five on the gym and forty on food. It's not much but with Callum on full pay we could get to two months' savings.

say: Five years is enough time for the government and the company to **plan properly**.
People should **start thinking now** rather than in 2030.
think: The office job still **goes before 2031** if the slow AI keeps improving.
Five years lets me **train for something** and wait for my boyfriend's apprenticeship to finish.
do: Stay a year or two and **save** while my boyfriend earns full wages.
Do the **healthcare assistant** course, then train in **taking blood**.
Use AI **more at work** so they keep me longer.
feel: **Anxious** but manageable, like knowing a storm is a week away, not an hour.
S3.quote: Five years is like knowing a storm's coming in a week, not an hour.
fieldNote: Time turns her plan into a **sequence**, saving first and then training.
She chooses **phlebotomy** for steady hands and calming nervous people.
She uses AI at work as a **holding tactic**, not as a future.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and eat out less to reach two months' savings
Train as a healthcare assistant, then as a phlebotomist
Use AI tools more at work to stay longer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not panic but let's not ignore it either. I think that's what most people at work would say. I'd say it at the pub quiz and at my mum's Sunday dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years helps a lot. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives, and if I've moved into the hospital by then I've got a few more years before robots. The insurance job still disappears, but I'd have time to go when I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am for a few years, get better at the job and the AI tools, and try for the bereavement team. Around thirty I'd start the healthcare training, ideally with the hospital paying for it. Callum and I might get married and buy a small place first, while I've still got an office salary for a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's far enough away that I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a place while you've still got the office salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because lenders like an office job with a payslip. If I'm a trainee healthcare assistant, I don't think they'd look at us. It's a bit sneaky, but that's how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm a bit of a 'wait and see' person. I'd want Callum to nudge me, and I'd tell myself thirty is the deadline. If I'm still scanning paper policies at thirty-two, something's gone wrong.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so let's not panic but let's not ignore it either.
I'd say that at the **pub quiz** and at my mum's Sunday dinner.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** at AGI, with a few years in the hospital before robots.
The insurance job still **disappears**, but I'd leave when I'm ready.
do: Stay a few years and try for the **bereavement team**.
Start **healthcare training** around thirty, ideally paid by the hospital.
Get married and **buy a small place** while I have an office salary.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay, far enough away to **breathe**.
S4.quote: If I'm still scanning paper policies at thirty-two, something's gone wrong.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the office job**, so the slow version stays anxious.
She times a **mortgage** around her office payslip, a sharp practical move.
She knows she tends to **wait and see** and sets herself a deadline.

steps.text: Apply to the bereavement claims team within two years
Start healthcare assistant training by age thirty
Marry Callum and buy a small flat on her office salary

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to retrain and we'd be living on Callum's apprentice wage. What would help is paid training into care, so I could earn while I learn. And some help with rent for a year, not forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people actually liked about their jobs. Mine's paperwork, but the bit I'd miss is the grieving people on the phone. If AI takes the death claims, someone should make sure the kindness doesn't go with it.

headlineQuote: If AI takes the death claims, someone should make sure the kindness doesn't go with it.
portrait: Iris is **twenty-seven** and handles policy changes and death claims at a life insurer's back office.
She lives with her boyfriend **Callum**, an apprentice electrician, on about three weeks' savings.
She is **pragmatic**, wants government to steer the change, and dislikes marches.
She takes up tools **after colleagues**, and her path out is **hands-on care** at the hospital.
Faster scenarios bring the hospital move forward, and slower ones let her **buy a home** first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to retrain and only an apprentice wage at home.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** into care so she can earn while learning.
**Help with rent** for a year while she switches.
